body:
On the contrary, I was just about to open an issue to not require a 3rd party font as a prerequisite. This should be just an opt-in.
I had an issue with this previously https://github.com/JetBrains/JetBrainsMono/issues/424 before realizing that I would have to change to use the Nerd Font to get the default icons working. This is not good.
Please reconsider the default behavior of starship.

Yes, agreed.
The deal breaker for me is that I would have to change my default monospace font to this NF, which Im not comfortable with. I just tried to add NF and `fc-cache -f -v` but it's not enough for the system to know about the glyph, you have to use the font, right? Not cool with that. Emoji is much more universal, therefore I would argue a better default.
But totally agree! Better to have a fully non-NF/NF switch, that what there is now.

@janos-r I don't get your aversion to NF. Just to be sure, are you aware that NF is not a specific font, but rather a "font patch" applicable to any font that replaces characters out of the usual ranges? If you use one of the popular programming fonts, there is probably already a pre-patched version here: https://www.nerdfonts.com/font-downloads, and if you don't, there is an easy tool to apply the patch to any local font: https://github.com/ryanoasis/nerd-fonts#font-patcher

@JanPokorny It's not always quite that simple. Sometimes the patcher fails, sometimes you have to do some work to figure out what font you're supposed to use (e.g. if I download a package called `nerd-fonts-source-code-pro`, it might be reasonable to assume that the font is called "Source Code Pro NF" or something, but this is totally wrong), and if you use CJK symbols on your system, NerdFonts might be unusable right now due to codepoints leaking out of the private-use area.

Admittedly that last one is a bug, but [it's been a bug for at least 18 months](https://github.com/ryanoasis/nerd-fonts/issues/365) and as far as I know, isn't about to be fixed in a hurry, since they need to do a major version upgrade to be able to push a breaking change like that.

But more generally, if you have a package manager that has Nerd Font packages and a terminal manager that lets you select fonts graphically, NerdFonts are dead simple to use. If your terminal is text-only config and you don't have access to package management (e.g. you don't have sudo), it gets a *lot* harder to set up if you haven't done it before. Lots of programmers don't understand the subtlety of fonts, shells, prompts, and the larger system--they just want a pretty shell that tells them useful information when they press ENTER.

@janos-r An interesting point is that this project has essentially always required a nerdcode font in the install instructions, but *de facto* didn't take advantage of it for a while. What finally forced our hand, believe it or not, was *inconsistency* of emoji. In particular, the cmake module (which has been a total thorn in terms of symbol selection) used to use a rounded triangle glyph for its symbol: 🛆

It turns out that this emoji is actually not supported by many fonts, and we didn't know this until we pushed the module out and started getting reports of breakage. To be fair, we could have spotted that issue for this particular emoji if we checked it on the emojipedia, but the point is that emoji support is often not the same from system to system, and it's hard to know in advance which ones are supported where.

To make life even more fun, display differences between emoji can make it much harder to scan the prompt. For example, on an old system I used, the camel emoji (for both the one-hump and two-hump camels) looked like this:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4605384/114222042-b1c82d80-9933-11eb-925e-d6c96171af48.png)

At 12pt font, I couldn't make out for the life of me what the heck this was supposed to be or what module it was supposed to be a part of. These kinds of inconsistencies generally do not occur with NerdFont symbols where you can (basically) guarantee that what the developer/tester sees is also what the user will ultimately see.

Alright, now that I have all those data points out there: I think this thread is generally right. I've been thinking for a while about how to support various stylings, and I think the solution is to create a way to dump the contents of an in-memory configuration and specify several defaults in the codebase itself (e.g. "NerdFont","Emoji","Plaintext"). Then you can have starship dump a particular default using some variant on `starship print-config`.

This is pretty much what clang-format does. It has several default styles (based on large companies/software projects) you can use to configure the code. You can also ask it to create a config file based on a particular style so that you can use it as a starting point (e.g. `clang-format -style=google -dump-config`).

We could even envision a `defaults` argument to the prompt command that will select options that are not explicitly configured by the config file from the appropriate default set.
I would settle for a single config option that sets all the symbols to the nerd font equivalents. Far nicer than manually applying this preset (looks more like a snippet to me).

I believe it makes sense for Starship default configuration to only use Powerline and emojis, but have a single `preset` setting that can be used to quickly switch all symbols to Nerd Font symbols or any other preset that is deemed good for inclusion by default by the developers.

Nerd Fonts are sadly problematic, with glyphs overlapping already used Unicode zones, breaking ligatures, etc. I was previously used them, but have since stopped due to such issues.

Out of the current default configuration, the following modules use Nerd Font symbols:
* `battery`
* `erlang`
* `node`
* `pulumi`

This is what I'm using to avoid Nerd Font symbols for now. If we can figure out proper icons for Erlang and Pulumi, and the maintainers say they are interested, I can make this into a PR that changes the defaults, moving the previous Nerd Font icons into the Nerd Font preset.
```toml
[battery]
full_symbol = "• "
charging_symbol = "⇡ "
discharging_symbol = "⇣ "
unknown_symbol = "❓ "
empty_symbol = "❗ "

[erlang]
symbol = "erl "

[nodejs]
symbol = "[⬢](bold green) "

#[pulumi]
#symbol = "pulumi "
```

@segevfiner Doesn't Starship also use Powerline symbols for Git (ie the branch symbol)? Powerline is a font mod (included in NerdFonts -- NF aggregates Powerline, Font Awesome and some more). If we want to make the default config "vanilla font friendly", these also need to go.

> @segevfiner Doesn't Starship also use Powerline symbols for Git (ie the branch symbol)? Powerline is a font mod (included in NerdFonts -- NF aggregates Powerline, Font Awesome and some more). If we want to make the default config "vanilla font friendly", these also need to go.

Yeah. This makes it friendly for Powerline, non Nerd Font. Those are more readily available and less buggy than the Nerd Fonts. Some fonts even include them by default or have official variations with them included (e.g. "Cascadia {Code,Mono} PL"). Most other fancy prompts like this one already require a Powerline font, e.g. spaceship prompt.

This is just getting more and more inconsistent... Now NodeJS uses a nerd font symbol too in master as far as I can tell.

It should either be Nerd Fonts by default with a plain symbols preset or plain symbols (Not plaintext) by default with a nerd fonts preset.

The default of a mixed Nerd Fonts and symbols and a full Nerd Fonts preset leaves those who want plain symbols without Nerd Fonts to cobble it up themselves.

And yes, not everyone would like to just install a Nerd Fonts due a to multitude of issues in them that are as of yet unresolved. Such as: Breaking ligatures in some fonts due to Unicode space collisions, Breaking other characters due to other Unicode space collisions, not supporting variable width fonts (The Cascadia variable font can't be patched properly, the static ones look way worse due to no manual hinting), breaking alignment of powerline characters, breaking font spacing and line width, and more and more. (All reported, just not fixed ATM, with very little activity in the repository)

@chipbuster @andytom @TrickyPi What do you think? 🤔
I didn't know that Nerd Fonts cause so much trouble. Perhaps I shouldn't even use them... This seems like a problem to solve in Unicode itself, doesn't it?

They can cause issue, it just depends on if you happen to hit a problem area in Unicode and the exact Nerd Font you are using. Just note that, as I stated, starship kinda arbitrarily uses them by default with no existing preset to switch to pure symbols. And that if they are working fine for you, then you can just keep using them, it's just a font so you can always switch later should it cause issues. The Nerd Font icons are nicer after all than just generic ones that look similar.

It's a problem to solve in the Nerd Fonts. They need to relocate to using purely the PUA areas intended for this, trying to choose ones that will conflict as minimally as possible with other popular users of the areas. This is a breaking change, and sadly very little has been done on the subject for a very long time.

Gonna break these responses up into a few sections to avoid a wall of text. First to respond to @segevfiner's initial paragraph:

> Now NodeJS uses a nerd font symbol too in master as far as I can tell.

It already did. We switched from one nerdfont symbol to another (in fact, from a misbehaving glyph to a better-behaved one). Here is the diff in my terminal, as a photo since diff display is dependent on browser font selection.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4605384/151749005-a3c9a6f2-984f-46ae-bdd9-4df270582ca5.png)

There is no visual difference in these diffs (when rendered in a terminal emulator that properly handles them), so as far as I'm concerned, the consistency of the prompt has not changed.

@mightyiam: As @segevfiner points out, this is an issue with NerdFonts. Unfortunately, I don't actually know if it's fixable at this point without causing major, major issues. The misbehaving codepoints will need to be moved, but this means that any application that relies on them will start displaying the wrong thing. Think about what happens if the application emits the byte sequence 0xAC 0x17 0x25 and this means "snake", but then one day this sequence now means "box". The thing being drawn by the terminal will suddenly change, *but the application doesn't get to see what's being drawn*, so it has no way of knowing something's wrong. Now multiply that by the hundreds of projects out there that have NerdFont dependencies...

If the application can't query the font being use (starship is in this category), then there's literally no way to detect the breakage---you'd just have to have a flag somewhere in the application that says "use NerdFonts v3" and then tell users to try switching back and forth between them if things are broken. It's a pretty nasty issue (and a little unfortunate that it snuck in).

On the topic at hand:

We currently don't provide a symbols-only preset. That's a problem and we should address it.

On this next point, I am not as certain:

> It should either be Nerd Fonts by default with a plain symbols preset or plain symbols (Not plaintext) by default with a nerd fonts preset.

There is definitely ideological simplicity in going all-in on one or the other, but does it actually translate into something that's always easier or better for us? For example, let's say we do a complete switch into NerdFonts by default. What if we can't find a ssuitable symbol for certain modules within the NF set? Scanning through quickly, I suspect there are not replacements for the jobs module, and I do not see things I find aesthetically pleasing for .NET or Dart.

Of course, this problem is even more exacerbated in emoji-land, where you hit several problems:

- You don't know what the emoji is going to look like on the user's system
- You don't know if the emoji is supported in the user's font
- Emojis were not designed to represent programming languages (surprise!) so the available space of symbols is often pretty small, leading to symbol reuse.

I agree that the NerdFont prerequisite is unfortunate, because it really puts off a lot of people who would otherwise like to use this terminal (I'm aware of at least one person in my personal sphere who wanted to try this, but got scared off by the font requirement).

This is all mostly just theorizing. I've personally become increasingly dissatisfied with the NerdFont requirement, especially because people will come to us for troubleshooting NerdFonts when the issue relaly is that their font fallback handling or emoji fonts are broken, and there seems to be a lot of troubleshooting energy spent on it. I actually recently [nuked all my patched fonts](https://github.com/starship/starship/discussions/1600#discussioncomment-1943729) and I'm only keeping the NerdFonts around for testing purposes.

@segevfiner Go ahead and open a PR with your proposed changes from [this comment](https://github.com/starship/starship/issues/2563#issuecomment-956007991) and we'll see what discussion is. Perhaps this will all be easier to resolve when we're looking at a concrete implementation rather than theorycrafting about potential solutions.

Finally, w.r.t. erlang and pulumi: I'm half-tempted to say that we should make "二郎" the emoji for erlang, but I suspect I'm the only person in the world who would find that amusing. On their website, their logo is just an "e", so maybe we could use a lowercase bold e for that? Or we could use one of the circle-inscribed ones like ⓔ?

As for pulumi, [their website](https://www.pulumi.com/) has lots of pretty dots on grids, so maybe we could co-opt a braille symbol for that.

Thanks for the response! 😃  (Walls of text go brrrrr!)

Thanks for letting me know you just switched one nerd font symbol to another. I just jumped to conclusions I guess, doesn't help that the browser can't render them on GitHub 😞 

Indeed fixing Nerd Fonts will be a big breaking change (A v3), there were issues where it was planned at some point, but no one knows when and if it will ever happens. And indeed there isn't a uniform way to query for the font AFAIK. (Maybe some arcane ANSI escape sequence exists? Who knows). Which will lead to compatibility flags as you said.

I did mean a preset/default that mostly uses Nerd Fonts but can use other available symbols if they look better, no real need to lock yourself to purely the additional Nerd Fonts symbols, it's just that the current situation is that you have some using Nerd Fonts symbols and some using plain symbols where a Nerd Font symbol is available, but I believe you got what I meant.

---

Should I make PR. Should it be one that changes the default to pure symbols and moves the Nerd Fonts ones to the Nerd Fonts preset? Or the other way around?

I'd say that making emoji default would be the best. Not all of our users actually have NerdFonts installed (if you're on a desktop and don't use Node/Erlang, you might not even realize that they're a requirement). It'll also be less work to move 4 modules into NerdFonts preset than it will be to make everything NerdFonts preset.

Could you also double-check the CMake default symbol when you do this? I swear I thought we moved it to a NerdFont symbol at some point, but maybe that got reverted.

Just chiming in as a potential new user interested in Starship who uses Source Code Pro in VS Code, and was put off by the NF variant saying it did not include all ligatures and glyphs. Those are a big reason I use this font in my editor, so I don't want to break my Code utility in order to experiment running a different terminal. I was interested enough in Starship to track down this issue, but there not being a default that doesn't require me to muck about with installed fonts is going to mean I pass for now.

@inlikealion You can use a different font for the terminal and editor in VSCode. And you can have NF and non-NF variants of fonts installed alongside. Also even if you use a non-NF fonts, there will be just a few icons missing, maybe you won't even notice since most programming fonts include Powerline (subset of NF) glyphs anyway
@inlikealion You can use my config snippet for the time being https://github.com/starship/starship/issues/2563#issuecomment-956007991 (Uncomment the `pulumi` section)

@JanPokorny Thanks for clarifying! I think this highlights that some attention to the README here could help new users understand and overcome the perceived barrier. @segevfiner Thanks! I'm going to take a leap and see if I can get it up and running without any conflicts.

One relevant thing I have discovered is that JetBrains IDEs (IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, CLion, Rider, ...) don't support emoji in the built-in terminal on Linux. (Their issue: https://youtrack.jetbrains.com/issue/IDEA-248010)

Nerd Fonts work correctly, though, so users of JetBrains IDEs on Linux are better off using the NF preset. Dropping it here since it seemed relevant for the debate.

Ad the debate about patched fonts -- it turns out many modern tools support font substitution, which means you can simply install the [NerdFonts symbols only](https://github.com/ryanoasis/nerd-fonts/releases/download/2.2.0-RC/NerdFontsSymbolsOnly.zip) font and the symbols will be substituted in all fonts (given the app supports it, I am not sure how prevalent this is across OSs). That could provide a much better installation experience -- the installation script could even install the icon font automatically.

AFAIK this partially works in Linux using fontconfig, but the resulting powerline/nerd glyphs are often badly aligned and/or sized, which made me prefer patched fonts. No idea how to set this up in this way in macOS and Windows. Generally this is even more complicated to install then just a plain patched font.
If you use wezterm as your terminal (win, linux, mac), it comes bundled with nerdfonts symbols only and uses it as a fallback.
